title: Is running the right computation sufficient for a mind?
question: If a machine ran exactly the computation your brain runs, would it have a mind, and would it feel anything?
status_reason: Thirteen reviewed works support sufficiency, twelve restrict it, four reject it, four decline to take sides; no reviewed work concedes to another.
status_scope: The corpus was built to trace this thesis, so both camps are over-represented relative to authors who never address it.

title: Does every ordinary object implement every computation?
question: If a rock can be described as running your brain's program, then saying a mind is a program says nothing. Does that follow?
status_reason: Chalmers's counterfactual-supporting conditionals plus combinatorial-state automata are not contested by any reviewed work; Piccinini calls the Putnam-Searle problem 'not very serious' (p. 281).
status_direction: toward the triviality objection failing once implementation conditions are stated modally
status_scope: Putnam 1988 and Searle 1990/1992, the sources of the objection, are not held; the corpus contains only its critics' reconstructions.

title: Which computation is a given system running, and does meaning decide?
question: One circuit can be called an AND gate or an OR gate depending on which voltage you call '1'. What fixes which computation a system is running?
status_reason: Non-semantic, mathematical-content, any-content, functional-equivalence-class and selection-history accounts all stand unreconciled in the corpus.
status_scope: Egan, Dewhurst, Haimovici and Piccinini 2008/2015 are known only through the papers that answer them.

title: How fine must functional equivalence be before it counts?
question: Copy a brain at what level of detail - whole regions, single neurons, synapses, molecules? Everyone needs an answer and nobody gives the same one.
status_reason: The corpus records at least eight distinct settings and two meta-positions saying the parameter cannot be fixed from human experiments; no reviewed work argues another's setting is wrong.
status_scope: This is the axis on which the field's disagreements actually turn, and no reviewed work proposes a run experiment that would settle it.

title: Does being alive matter, and in which of its three non-equivalent senses?
question: Is a mind something only a living thing can have - and if so, is it metabolism, bodily self-regulation, or specific brain wiring that does the work?
status_reason: The biological works lower the thesis's plausibility without rejecting it; Chalmers calls the requirement 'biological chauvinism' while assigning it a one-in-three credence.
status_scope: Nobody in the reviewed biological batch rejects computational functionalism; Thompson 2007, the hub all three biological works cite, is not held.

title: Can theories of consciousness be tested at all, and does the thesis gate which theories count?
question: Every measurement of consciousness runs through a report. Can any theory survive that, and is 'computation suffices' now used to decide which theories get assessed?
status_reason: Doerig's and Kleiner's formal results stand unanswered in the corpus, while Butlin et al. proceed by excluding the theory that denies the thesis (p. 5, p. 33).
status_scope: The published replies to the unfolding argument (Kleiner 2020; Tsuchiya, Andrillon & Haun 2019) are named but not held.

title: Is what a system says or does evidence about whether it has a mind?
question: A chatbot trained on human talk can say it feels things. Is that evidence, and if not, what is?
status_reason: Six reviewed works independently downgrade behaviour and upgrade architecture; Birch's gaming problem and Shevlin's gerrymandered robot give the general form.
status_direction: toward architectural rather than behavioural evidence, at least for trained systems
status_scope: Long et al. share two authors (Chalmers, Birch) with works they cite for this, so the convergence is partly co-authorship rather than independent agreement.

title: Are today's language models candidates for minds?
question: Does anything in a large language model make it a serious candidate for having experiences?
status_reason: Every reviewed work that gives a verdict says no current system is a strong candidate; they split sharply on whether the obstacles are temporary.
status_direction: toward no current system being a strong candidate, with the trajectory question wide open
status_scope: The corpus holds no work arguing at length against AI moral status from inside the AI-minds literature; opponents appear only as reported objections.

title: What should be done while the question stays open?
question: If nobody can settle whether a machine feels anything, who decides how to treat it, and on what evidence?
status_reason: Four procedural recommendations are on the table and they do not compose: do-not-build, corporate assess-and-prepare, a roadmap-or-red-flags list, and citizen-panel precaution.
status_scope: Birch's framework is read here from the published precis, not the book; the assessed policy proposals (Bryson, Metzinger) are named only.
